Chapter 5: Leading and Parenting with Openness and Trust
You know, leadership and parenting often come with the unspoken expectation that you’re supposed to have all the answers. There’s this pressure to look strong, decisive, and always in control.
But here’s the real secret—the most effective leaders and parents? They’re the ones who aren’t afraid to be vulnerable. They create spaces where trust, learning, and real connection can actually happen.
Imagine a manager facing a major setback. Instead of pointing fingers or pretending everything’s fine, she brings her team together, opens up about her concerns, and asks for their ideas.
At first, the team’s a little surprised by her honesty. But then, something shifts. People start sharing, offering support, and brainstorming solutions. That setback? It turns into a chance for everyone to grow—not just the project, but the team’s sense of unity.
Most folks think that showing vulnerability as a leader is risky. Like, it’ll make you look weak or open the door to criticism. But honestly, the opposite is usually true. When leaders are upfront about challenges and own their mistakes, they actually build trust.
Teams feel more engaged, they’re more willing to take initiative, and they bounce back faster when things get tough.
Parenting’s really no different. Every parent wants to protect their child from pain or failure. That urge is strong. But if you shield kids from every struggle, you take away their chance to build resilience.
Picture a parent watching their child wrestle with a tough task. Instead of swooping in to fix everything, she offers a few words of encouragement and just listens. The child might get frustrated, but sticks with it—and eventually figures things out.
That sense of pride and confidence? It’s hard-won—and it lasts.
Openness in parenting also means being willing to say, “I’m sorry.” When a parent loses patience or makes a mistake, admitting it teaches kids that nobody’s perfect. It models what accountability looks like and reminds them that love isn’t about being flawless.
Whether you’re leading a team or raising a child, trust comes from being consistent, showing empathy, and being willing to be real. It’s about creating a space where people feel safe to speak up, to take chances, and to learn—even when things don’t go as planned.
I think of a teacher, new to her classroom, struggling to connect with her students. Instead of just sticking to the lesson plan, she starts sharing her own learning journey—the ups, the doubts, even her small wins.
And in response, the students open up about their own challenges. Suddenly, the classroom feels different. There’s real respect and curiosity in the air.
This journey isn’t about being perfect. It’s about showing up, even when it’s tough, and inviting others to do the same.
When leaders and parents embrace vulnerability, they build cultures of trust, innovation, and a true sense of belonging.
Of course, the work never really ends. There’ll be moments of doubt, and sometimes those old habits of control or perfectionism sneak back in.
But every time you choose openness over armor, that foundation of trust gets a little stronger.
And in the end, it’s not just about having better teams or happier families—it’s about feeling more connected and finding a deeper sense of purpose together.
